name: Guyana
summary_text: Guyana criminalises consensual same-sex conduct under the Criminal Law (Offences) Act 1893, retained in force after independence. Section 351 punishes gross indecency between men with up to two years imprisonment. Section 353 punishes buggery with life imprisonment, with related provisions covering attempted buggery. Some compilations cite the same offences as sections 352 to 354.  Prosecutions under these provisions are rare. The statutes nevertheless structure police encounters with lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons and sustain public stigma.  A constitutional savings clause bars judicial review of laws inherited at independence. The clause prevents courts from invalidating the inherited sexual offences even where they conflict with human rights guarantees.  Guyana provides no procedure for legal gender recognition. No provision for change of gender marker was identified in the sources.  The direct prohibition on cross-dressing, section 153(1)(xlvii) of the Summary Jurisdiction (Offences) Act derived from an 1893 statute, was struck down on 13 November 2018. A regional court held in Quincy McEwan, Seon Clarke, Joseph Fraser, Seyon Persaud and SASOD v The Attorney General of Guyana that the provision was unconstitutionally vague, violated protection of the law and was contrary to freedom of expression and the rule of law. The case followed arrests of transgender women in 2009 with three nights detention, a challenge filed in 2010 with support from transgender and gay advocacy groups, a 2013 Chief Justice ruling that permitted cross-dressing unless for an improper purpose, affirmance by the Court of Appeal, and oral argument before the regional court beginning 28 June 2018.  Police abuse linked to the remaining laws is documented. The managing director of SASOD, Joel Simpson, reported in May 2019 that officers threatened men found in compromising positions with arrest under the sodomy laws to extract bribes, harassed same-sex couples in public spaces including seawalls and parks, and subjected complainants to secondary discrimination at stations. As a result complainants gave watered down accounts. Hate crimes often go unreported. After the 2018 ruling, residual loitering and vagrancy clauses remained usable against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons, principally sex workers.  Transgender women face documented street violence and failure of judicial protection. Petronella Trotman was stabbed in Georgetown in January 2017, sustaining a neck wound inflicted with scissors alongside an attack with glass bottles. On 2 March 2017 a magistrate, Dylon Bess, refused her entry to the Georgetown Magistrates Court unless she was dressed like a man. Her case against her attacker was then dismissed.  A hearing at the 191st session of the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, requested by the Guyana Equality Forum on the impact of gender-based violence on migrant women, sex workers and transgender women, heard testimony from Blossom Inc., SASOD and the Guyana Sex Work Coalition. The Commission chair, Roberta Clarke, called on Guyana on 16 November 2024 to take urgent action. The record cited 69 documented cases of violence against trans women between 2018 and 2022.  Same-sex marriage and civil unions do not exist in Guyana. Constitutional protection on the ground of sexual orientation, approved unanimously in December 2000, was denied presidential assent before the March 2001 elections after religious opposition, and a reintroduction in 2003 was withdrawn without progress.  No hate-crime legislation covering sexual orientation and gender identity exists. On 16 June 2019 Simpson was beaten by six men after harassment at the Palm Court nightclub while waiting at Bourda Market. He filed a police complaint and called for hate-crime legislation. The Ministry of Social Protection condemned the attack while affirming acceptance. In July 2019 the Court of Appeal reduced a 57-year murder sentence imposed in 2015 on Clive Knights for the 2012 killing of Bert Whyte to 30 years for manslaughter after a claim of unwanted homosexual advances. Discrimination and violence by law enforcement, religious leaders and others are described as widespread, leading most lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons to conceal their orientation.  Official statements in favour of protection have not changed the statute book. In July 2019 Minister of Social Protection Amna Ally stated the government was working to remove legal gaps to prevent discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity and affirmed the right to live free from violence, abuse and discrimination. In July 2025 five of six main parties, including the ruling party, supported decriminalisation. In September 2025 President Irfaan Ali promised to decriminalise in cooperation with SASOD. The criminal provisions remained in force.

name: Honduras
summary_text: Nothing in Honduran law criminalises gender identity. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in Honduras since 1899, with the age of consent set at 15 years for both same-sex and heterosexual conduct.  The Penal Code, amended by Decree No. 23-2013 and in force since March 2017, treats hatred or contempt based on sexual orientation or gender identity as an aggravating circumstance for criminal responsibility under Article 27. Article 321 punishes anyone who arbitrarily blocks, restricts or denies individual or collective rights or refuses a professional service on those grounds with three to five years imprisonment and a fine of four to seven minimum wages. Article 321-A punishes public or media incitement to discrimination, hatred, contempt, persecution, violence or attacks on those grounds with three to five years imprisonment and a fine of L.50,000 to L.300,000. The provisions were retained in the new Code after LGBTI rights groups met with Congress on the wording.  The 2001 Law on Police and Social Affairs permits arrest of anyone who goes against modesty, proper conduct and public morals. LGBTI organizations have documented numerous instances in which police have used this provision as a pretext to harass and detain transgender women, restricting their access to public space.  Human Rights Watch reported in May 2009 that police in Honduras subjected transgender people to rape, assault and extortion. International human rights organizations have stated that the military government targeted LGBTI people for harassment, abuse and murder.  Honduras holds transgender women in the men's penitentiary system, with no placement by gender identity policy. At Penitenciaria Nacional Tamara, LGBTI prisoners are concentrated in the La Isla module beside the unit for mentally ill prisoners. Trans women there are forced to cut their hair, barred from presenting as women and denied conjugal visits. At Penitenciaria de Marcala, authorities seized a trans woman's clothes and cut her hair, and only after intervention by the torture prevention centre CPTRT was she separated from men and her belongings returned.  Human Rights Watch confirmed in 2020 that Honduras places transgender women in men's prisons, which can lead to physical and sexual abuse. A Honduran judge described a case in which a trans woman was raped by fellow detainees with the complicity of guards. The judge had informed prosecutors, who did not investigate.  Same-sex unions are not legally recognized. A 2005 constitutional amendment bans same-sex marriage and de facto unions, refuses recognition of same-sex marriages or unions legally performed in other countries under Article 112, and prohibits adoption by same-sex couples under Article 116. Same-sex couples lack the legal protections available to opposite-sex married couples.  Registered violence includes 69 transgender persons among 174 violent LGBTI deaths between 2009 and 2014, and 264 LGBTI people murdered between 2009 and 2017, concentrated in Cortes and Francisco Morazan. Transgender activist Cynthia Nicole was shot dead on 2 January, and trans activist Thalia Rodriguez was murdered on 10 January 2022 in Tegucigalpa. In June 2013 Spain granted asylum to a transsexual woman from Honduras after a police officer attempted to assassinate her. Vicky Hernandez v. Honduras, heard at the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, is the leading transfemicide case.  Impunity is structural. LGBTI persons, particularly trans women, face major obstacles to justice linked to under-reporting, lack of police and prosecutor training, insufficient resources and intentional mishandling of cases. The United States Department of State 2021 Human Rights Report listed violence and threats against LGBTQI+ persons, extrajudicial killings, torture, corruption and lack of accountability for gender-based violence.  Official hostility is on record. President Juan Orlando Hernandez said on 12 October 2018 that as a Christian he was personally against same-sex marriage. The president of the Tegucigalpa Pastors Association urged President Xiomara Castro to stop immoral laws. The two major parties have largely ignored LGBTI rights.

At Penitenciaria de Marcala, authorities seized a trans woman's clothes and cut her hair, and only after intervention by the torture prevention centre CPTRT was she separated from men and her belongings returned.  Human Rights Watch confirmed in 2020 that Honduras places transgender women in men's prisons, which can lead to physical and sexual abuse. A Honduran judge described a case in which a trans woman was raped by fellow detainees with the complicity of guards. The judge had informed prosecutors, who did not investigate.  Same-sex unions are not legally recognized. A 2005 constitutional amendment bans same-sex marriage and de facto unions, refuses recognition of same-sex marriages or unions legally performed in other countries under Article 112, and prohibits adoption by same-sex couples under Article 116. Same-sex couples lack the legal protections available to opposite-sex married couples.  Registered violence includes 69 transgender persons among 174 violent LGBTI deaths between 2009 and 2014, and 264 LGBTI people murdered between 2009 and 2017, concentrated in Cortes and Francisco Morazan. Transgender activist Cynthia Nicole was shot dead on 2 January, and trans activist Thalia Rodriguez was murdered on 10 January 2022 in Tegucigalpa. In June 2013 Spain granted asylum to a transsexual woman from Honduras after a police officer attempted to assassinate her. Vicky Hernandez v. Honduras, heard at the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, is the leading transfemicide case.  Impunity is structural. LGBTI persons, particularly trans women, face major obstacles to justice linked to under-reporting, lack of police and prosecutor training, insufficient resources and intentional mishandling of cases. The United States Department of State 2021 Human Rights Report listed violence and threats against LGBTQI+ persons, extrajudicial killings, torture, corruption and lack of accountability for gender-based violence.  Official hostility is on record. President Juan Orlando Hernandez said on 12 October 2018 that as a Christian he was personally against same-sex marriage. The president of the Tegucigalpa Pastors Association urged President Xiomara Castro to stop immoral laws. The two major parties have largely ignored LGBTI rights.
